task: Imagina que en tu edificio o escuela quieren hacer un jardín en la terraza. Escribe un mensaje de 80–100 palabras a los vecinos con ventajas, posibles problemas y una propuesta concreta.
paragraphs: Look up the next time you walk through a big city. Above the shops and offices, there may be a garden. In cities such as New York, Paris and Singapore, more and more roofs are being covered with plants, vegetables and even beehives.

Rooftop gardens are not just pretty. A roof covered with plants absorbs rainwater, so less water runs into the streets during heavy storms. The plants also keep buildings cooler in summer and warmer in winter, which can reduce the energy needed for air conditioning and heating. In addition, they provide a home for birds, butterflies and bees.

Some rooftop gardens are businesses. In Brooklyn, one farm grows tons of vegetables every year on top of old industrial buildings and sells them to local restaurants and families. Other gardens are run by volunteers who share the harvest. On the roof of a hospital in Boston, staff grow vegetables that are served to patients.

However, creating a garden on a roof is not as easy as it sounds. The building has to be strong enough to support the weight of soil, water and people. The roof must be completely waterproof, and the gardeners need to think about strong winds and intense sun. All this can be expensive, so some cities offer grants or tax reductions to building owners who install green roofs.

For many city dwellers, the biggest benefit is not the vegetables but the experience. "After work, I come up here, pull out a few weeds and forget about my emails," says Lena, who looks after a small plot on a roof in Berlin. "I've met more neighbours here than in ten years of living in this building."
